stated.value: We already have a fluorescence spectrometer and would like to use it
We have not identified a fluorescent target, marker or reference relationship
report glucose concentration and viable biomass directly during fermentation

missing: Glucose concentration range and required accuracy
How viable biomass is defined and measured in the laboratory (reference method)
Bioreactor type, probe port, temperature and sterilisation requirements
Model and spectral range of the existing fluorescence spectrometer and excitation source

status_reason: Material (fermentation), quantities (glucose, viable biomass) and location (during fermentation) are stated, but the fluorescence concept for both targets is not supported by the sources, so only a provisional assessment with an alternative method to test is possible.
answer: Sensitivity alone does not justify fluorescence: it is rated low in selectivity, works only for fluorescent components, and in the supplied bioprocess material glucose is assigned to NIR and Raman while fluorescence targets NADH, tryptophan and riboflavin. Test Raman (with NIR as comparison) for glucose first, and treat your fluorescence spectrometer at most as a supporting signal for biomass combined with NIR, validated against an independent viable-cell reference.

inline.headline: Test Raman for glucose in the fermentation broth, compared with NIR, before any in-line installation.
inline.probe: Raman fiber probe with filters designed to suppress laser scatter and fluorescence
inline.install: Initially on laboratory fermentation samples, later in a bioreactor port once the client defines it
inline.fiber: Vis-NIR silica (350-2400 nm), preferably Al/Cu-coated to avoid polymer-jacket fluorescence; excitation wavelength and Raman shift range to be defined in the test
inline.not_final_because: The organism, medium, glucose range, accuracy requirement, bioreactor port and a viable-biomass reference are unknown, Raman can be masked by fluorescence of organic compounds, and a published application is only a reason to test.

problems.text: High sensitivity is not selectivity: fluorimetry is rated high in sensitivity but low in selectivity and only works when the sample has a fluorescent component, which you have not identified.
There is no direct fluorescence route to glucose in the sources: fluorescence targets NADH, tryptophan and riboflavin, while glucose is assigned to NIR and Raman.

Viable biomass needs a defined signal and reference: the sources link biomass to turbidity (cell density) and report better biomass estimates from NIR plus fluorescence, but describe no viable-cell measurement, so an independent viability reference is required.
Fluorescence, NIR and UV give broad overlapping spectra, so any quantitative result needs a chemometric model built and validated against reference analyses.

methods.why: Raman gives direct detection of glucose, acetate or lactate and suits aqueous media because water absorbs weakly.
NIR tracks major components such as glucose in the millimolar range and is the most common online fiber-probe method, but may lack sensitivity below 0.1 %.
UV/Vis turbidity correlates with cell density and can be a low-cost biomass indicator, with probe choice depending on optical density.

Fluorescence is suitable for intrinsic fluorophores such as NADH, tryptophan and riboflavin and may support biomass only in combination with NIR, not as a stand-alone glucose or viability measurement.

questions.q: How do you measure viable biomass in the laboratory today, and can you provide those reference values for fermentation samples?
questions.why: The sources describe no viable-cell measurement, so a model needs an independent viability reference.

questions.q: Which organism and medium do you use, and what glucose concentration range must be reported with what accuracy?
questions.why: NIR tracks glucose in the millimolar range but may lack sensitivity below 0.1 %, which decides between NIR and Raman.

questions.q: Which excitation wavelength and spectral range does your fluorescence spectrometer cover?
questions.why: Fluorescence only helps if an intrinsic fluorophore such as NADH, tryptophan or riboflavin is excited and detected.

questions.q: Which bioreactor port, temperature and sterilisation conditions must an in-line probe withstand?
questions.why: Each method needs its own probe interface and the task decides the technique.

questions.q: How turbid is the broth at the end of fermentation?
questions.why: Optical density decides between transmission/transflection and other probe types.

experiment.objective: Find out whether Raman or NIR sees glucose changes in your fermentation broth and whether NIR plus fluorescence tracks biomass against an independent reference.
steps: Collect fermentation samples across the run, covering the expected glucose and biomass ranges.
Measure each sample with Raman and NIR fiber probes and record fluorescence with your existing spectrometer at the same time.
Analyse every sample independently in the laboratory for glucose and for viable biomass with your reference method.
Build chemometric models per method and for the NIR plus fluorescence combination, and validate them on samples not used for calibration.
references: Independent laboratory viable-biomass analysis defined by the client

pathway.key_features: No spectra were supplied; key spectral features for glucose and biomass must be identified by multivariate analysis of the laboratory test data.
pathway.path_reason: The multi-method lab test and key-feature selection must come before a chemometric model, customised system or sensor.

multispectral.why: NIR tracks major components while fluorescence detects intrinsic fluorophores reflecting the metabolic state, and this combination gave more accurate biomass in yeast fermentation.
multispectral.probe: separate synchronised probes, unless the broth proves heterogeneous, in which case a combined multispectral probe is needed to see the same spot
multispectral.fusion: low-level fusion of synchronised spectra with a dedicated data-fusion algorithm, compared with a model per method
multispectral.test: The fused model must predict the biomass reference better than the best single-method model on the same independent validation samples.

assumptions: The fermentation broth is an aqueous medium.
Independent laboratory reference analyses for glucose and viable biomass can be provided by the client.
